While reading, I kept coming back to the idea "why can't they devise permanent containment?" Individuals are sub-human intelligence outside a two digit flock, so anything sufficient to contain a human should work fine. A bit easier than that since they don't have thumbs.

A note that containment should be treated as akin to an escape-risk humanoid rather than zoo-like would be sufficient in-universe and achieve the same literary effect.

item.content:encoded: While I love the idea, I find it seriously hard to believe the foundation is unable to contain a bunch of physically normal birds because they are "too smart". Knock them out and build a solid titanium rib cage around them with holes too small for them to fit through by a significant margin. With that, brains don't matter at all; escape is impossible. A bunch of exceedingly low tech containment solutions are easily available.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
But the point here, my dear doctor, is that this, like the geth, is not a single consciousness, a "group mind" - each individual retains full individuality. It's just that the more individuals there are in close proximity, the more intelligent each individual becomes. In Mass Effect 2, had Shepard decided to eradicate, say, 50% of the programs running on Legion's platform, the remaining individuals comprising the Legion platform would have been operating at about half their starting capacity.

Group minds are certainly common, as are intelligent individuals with telepathic awareness - the habitues of Callahan's Place and its successors have done this, and even increased their available time to think (almost the same thing as increasing effective IQ) by sharing available processing capacity in each others' brains - but the sort of additive intellect used by these birds is quite uncommon. It may well have been done before, but I'm willing to wager that for those here who have been exposed to the idea previously, said exposure did indeed have to do with the geth. (For instance, despite a lifeline fascination with SF, I was unaware of Hamilton's Edenists.)

I further submit that several of the entries under "non-hive minds" in that Wikipedia article do not belong there - the Fleetmind in Schlock Mercenary, for instance, isn't really a single mind, it's just that the AIs involved turn off the subroutines that slow them down to organic speeds while they communicate, and can thus act and think with greater speed than their "meat glacier" friends, while the Little People in Methuselah's Children, while they do maintain the memories in the group, no longer display the personalities of the individuals absorbed.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm not going to hazard a guess as to the origin of "group mind", but the idea of the "group mind" becoming stronger and/or more intelligent with more individuals in physical proximity seems to flow naturally from it. I can promise that Mass Effect (or any other video game) did not originate the concept.

It's a long, long list.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's not reminding you of anything in Foundation custody.

It's reminding you of the geth. In my not-so-very-damned-humble opinion, this is not necessarily a bad thing - the concept of geth intelligence, that in a group they became smarter but did not share any sort of "hive mind", seems to have been original with Mass Effect (leading to such wonders as Legion, at one point in the sequel, needing to poll all the programs running in its platform as to the best course of action…).

I think I like these birds, but I need to let the idea mull for a while first.
